beats.trigger: Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: There is homework I will not have done.

beats.trigger: **Distinguish** compliant, violating and "I can't tell" for each rule
beats.got: Three outcomes per rule, one of them an honest 'don't know'. That's more than I expected.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked what I'd check first, not told.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent's words become actions through a harness, and a bad description or bad context carries through to the action. I can see why that's a security question.

beats.trigger: Leading companies are investing in enablement programmes, champions networks and training, and the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old security assumed the same input gives the same output. Fine, I know that.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: The attack is a sentence in a document the agent reads, not an exploit in code. That is new, and my IT security people would care.

beats.trigger: Clear communication, strong sponsorship and regular follow-up remain the foundation, and agents are simply one more area where those principles apply.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: This is a rapidly evolving area, and organisations of every size are working out how best to approach it.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the same paragraph as before.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: Safety costs usefulness, and somebody has to pick the trade and sign for it. They say so plainly.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The best control is not connecting the thing, and it costs a feature. A straight admission, which I don't often get.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years.
beats.got: nothing new. It's the 2017 slide.

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a saved check you can run again. Makes sense, a bit like a checklist.

beats.trigger: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent ran our policy files against the system I built and split the rules into checkable and not checkable. I can test that myself.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell it what actually matters here and challenge the generic output. I'm in control, which I like.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: Company policy is one lens and agent risk is the other. It's a long interview.

beats.trigger: You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer.
beats.got: Answer what I know and hand back the rest. Practical.

beats.trigger: The skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: Install steps. Plumbing.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: This adds to our existing controls and doesn't replace them. Good, nobody gets told the security department is obsolete.

beats.trigger: Clear communication, strong sponsorship and regular follow-up remain the foundation
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Check that the skill shows up.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit gives me a report with rows flagged and things it can't judge, on a system I built. I can verify it row by row.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The risk report left me uneasy about my own system, and they say that unease is the point. That is honest.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new. Third time I've seen this paragraph.

beats.trigger: Sometimes the right next step is not another prompt.
beats.got: When the agent can't tell, take the evidence to legal or security with one narrow question. Sensible and co-determination-friendly.

beats.trigger: We did this for one risk.
beats.got: One risk handled is a prototype. A production agent needs all of them done. They admit the limit.

beats.trigger: the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: "That residual is too vague, name the file or behaviour."
beats.got: The agent writes rules into the instructions file from what happened, and I push back on vague ones. Reasonable.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills can be reused for other recurring checks and passed to colleagues. Ownership is left open.

beats.trigger: Remember that success with AI is everyone's responsibility.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework, and a nudge. I will probably not do it.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases of agent output going wrong with no check around it. Those I would read.

take_homes: Agents can be attacked with plain sentences in documents they read. This is a different kind of risk from code exploits.
The safest control is not opening the door, and it costs a feature. Someone has to pick the trade and sign for it.
A checking agent gave me a report on my own system with 'can't tell' rows I could verify myself. I would show that to my security people.

monday.move: Probably nothing myself. If I act, I forward the risk-report idea and the 'door you don't open' point to our security lead and ask whether they would run the check on one existing automation.
monday.when: Sometime next week, after the steering group backlog
monday.stop_condition: They say it duplicates what they already do, or the first report is generic
monday.blocker: My calendar, the previous programme's steering groups, and the unsolved question of who owns an agent.

misconception.why: The sentence-as-attack point and the admission that the best control costs a feature are not in the agile or OKR decks. I still read the 'A note on context' paragraphs as the same old slide, and they are the reason I'd say wait and see for the rest of the programme. But the security part is a real change, not just a slide.

one_line: Roughly half of it is real and the other half is 2017 filler. The part where you run the audit on your own system and it admits what it can't tell is the real half, and it's worth an hour.
